title: System Design Fundamentals
summary: Scale, latency, availability, and what breaks when the network splits — the handful of ideas behind every design interview and every outage.

blocks.markdown:
System design is picking components and connections so a system is fast, handles load, stays up, and stays correct enough — on a budget.

- **Scaling** — handle more load: a bigger machine (vertical) or more machines (horizontal).
- **Latency** — time for one request. **Throughput** — requests finished per second. Different knobs.
- **Availability** — fraction of time it works, measured in "nines."
- **Consistency** — do all readers see the latest write? A spectrum, not a yes/no.
- The standard toolkit is small: load balancer, cache, queue, database, CDN, object store.

blocks.subTitle: What to reach for
blocks.markdown:
Match the need to the tool — most designs are these six pieces arranged sensibly.

| Need | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Lower read latency on hot data | Cache |
| Slow work the user shouldn't wait on | Queue / async |
| One server can't take the traffic | Horizontal scaling + LB |
| Must never serve wrong data (money) | Strong consistency, CP |
| Must always respond, stale OK (likes) | High availability, AP |

blocks.subTitle: Vertical vs horizontal scaling
blocks.markdown:
Two ways to handle more load: a stronger box, or more boxes.

![Vertical versus horizontal scaling](assets/system-design-fundamentals/vertical-vs-horizontal-scaling.svg)

- **Vertical (scale up)** — more CPU, RAM, disk on one machine. Simple, no code change, but a hard ceiling and still a single point of failure.
- **Horizontal (scale out)** — many nodes behind a load balancer. Near-limitless, but needs stateless servers and coordination.
- Rule: start vertical, go horizontal *before* you hit the ceiling.

blocks.subTitle: Latency vs throughput
blocks.markdown:
Latency is how long one request takes; throughput is how many you finish per second. They are independent knobs.

- Report latency in **percentiles** (p99), not averages — the slow tail is what users feel.
- **Batching** raises throughput (less per-item overhead) but raises latency (each item waits for the batch).
- Memory is ~1000x faster than SSD; SSD ~100x faster than a cross-country hop; an ocean crossing costs ~150ms no matter what.
- That speed gap is *why* caches and CDNs exist — they move data closer.

blocks.subTitle: Availability & nines
blocks.markdown:
Availability is the fraction of time the system serves correctly, written in "nines."

| Nines | Downtime / year |
|---|---|
| 99% (two) | ~3.65 days |
| 99.9% (three) | ~8.8 hours |
| 99.99% (four) | ~52 minutes |

Each extra nine is ~10x harder. It comes from **redundancy** plus fast failure detection and failover. Series dependencies multiply and get *worse* (0.99 x 0.99 = 98%); redundant copies multiply failure odds and get *better*.

blocks.subTitle: Statelessness & SPOFs
blocks.markdown:
A **stateless** server keeps no per-client data in local memory between requests — state lives in a shared store.

- Statelessness is the *precondition* for horizontal scaling: any node serves any request, you add or kill nodes freely.
- Push sessions to Redis, files to an object store, durable data to the DB; keep the app tier stateless.
- A **single point of failure (SPOF)** is any one component whose death stops everything — a lone DB, single LB, one zone.
- Find them: walk the request path and ask "what if this dies?" Add redundancy where the answer is "everything stops."

blocks.subTitle: CAP & PACELC
blocks.markdown:
When the network splits, you can't have both consistency and availability.

![CAP theorem triangle](assets/system-design-fundamentals/cap-theorem-triangle.svg)

- **CAP** — at most two of Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance. Partitions are unavoidable, so **P is mandatory**; the real choice is **C vs A during a partition**.
- **CP** refuses possibly-stale answers (bank ledger); **AP** answers anyway (social feed).
- **PACELC** — if Partition, choose A or C; **Else**, choose Latency or Consistency. Strong consistency costs latency even on a healthy network ([consistency-replication](consistency-replication)).

blocks.subTitle: The consistency spectrum
blocks.markdown:
"Consistent or not" is a beginner's framing — consistency is a dial.

- **Strong / linearizable** — every read sees the latest write everywhere. Easiest to reason about, costs latency.
- **Read-your-own-writes** — you always see your own changes; others may lag.
- **Monotonic reads** — you never see time go backwards.
- **Eventual** — replicas converge once writes stop. Cheapest and most available, but a read may be stale now.
- The skill: match the level per feature. Bank balance needs strong; a "viewed by" count is fine eventual.

blocks.subTitle: The standard stack
blocks.markdown:
Almost every backend is six reusable pieces arranged in one shape.

![Scalable web architecture](assets/system-design-fundamentals/scalable-web-architecture.svg)

- **Load balancer** spreads requests across **stateless app servers** and skips dead ones.
- **Cache** holds hot data in memory; **queue** decouples slow work from the request path.
- **Database** is the durable source of truth; **object store** holds large blobs (S3); **CDN** serves static bytes from the edge.
- The backbone: client to CDN to LB to app tier to cache / queue / DB / object store.

blocks.subTitle: The axes you trade on
blocks.markdown:
Every design moves along a few axes — name them out loud in interviews.

- **Simplicity vs scalability** — a monolith is easy but caps out; distributed scales but adds coordination and failure modes.
- **Latency vs consistency** — strong consistency waits for agreement; weak answers now but may be stale.
- **Availability vs consistency** — the CAP choice during partitions.
- **Cost vs redundancy** — each nine, replica, and cache layer costs money and ops.
- **Read vs write** — caches and replicas speed reads but make writes propagate and invalidate.

blocks.subTitle: Rules of thumb
blocks.markdown:
Plain-English defaults that get you most of the way.

- Data is **money, inventory, auth** then strong consistency / CP, accept the latency.
- Data is a **feed, count, recommendation** then availability / eventual, optimize latency.
- **Reads far outnumber writes** then add a **cache** for the hot set, then **read replicas**; keep writes on a primary.
- Slow task the user doesn't need now then push it to a **queue** ([messaging-streaming](messaging-streaming)).
- Static or distant content then put a **CDN** in front.
- Tempted to make a server remember things then don't; push state to a shared store.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems & the method
blocks.markdown:
The same dials show up in the systems you use, and one loop tackles any design question.

- **DynamoDB** — AP, eventual by default, opt-in strong reads (per-request PACELC).
- **Spanner** — CP, globally strong via TrueTime clocks; writes wait out a small uncertainty window.
- **Netflix** — CDN at planetary scale, stateless tier across zones, Chaos Monkey to prove no SPOFs.
- **Postgres read replicas** — reads scale out; the cost is **replication lag** (a stale read after your write).
- The loop: clarify, estimate scale, define API, model data, sketch architecture, drill the hard part, address failure & trade-offs.

The misconceptions that sink interviews and designs:

- **"Scaling means a bigger server."** Vertical has a hard ceiling and stays a SPOF; past a point you *must* go horizontal.
- **"CAP lets me pick CA."** Partitions aren't optional, so P is always on — the real choice is C vs A during one.
- **"Consistency is on or off."** It's a spectrum; tune it per feature.
- **"Caching is free."** It adds staleness, invalidation, and stampedes — a trade, not a freebie.
- **"Average latency tells the story."** Averages hide the tail; reason in p95/p99.
- **"Stateless stores nothing."** It stores no *per-client* state *locally* — shared stores still hold state.
